questions.question: Describe the geography of South Africa's conventional energy production — where the thermal stations are and why, what limits hydro-electricity, and how pumped storage schemes work and why the grid needs them.
questions.expected_answer: Roughly eight in every ten units of South African electricity come from coal burned in thermal stations — Tutuka, Duvha, Kendal, Matimba, Medupi and Kusile among them — clustered directly on the Mpumalanga, Waterberg and Free State coalfields, because moving electricity along high-voltage lines costs far less than hauling coal by rail; the coal stays put and the power travels, mostly toward Gauteng. Koeberg's nuclear output, hydro and pumped storage schemes and growing renewables share the remaining slice. True hydro-electricity stays small because rainfall is low and rivers are seasonal, so reliable falling water is scarce: the Gariep and Vanderkloof stations on the Orange River generate at peak times, and additional hydro-power is imported from Cahora Bassa on the Zambezi in Mozambique. Pumped storage schemes like Palmiet, Steenbras and Ingula pair a high dam with a low one: in the small hours surplus cheap grid power pumps water to the top dam, and at the evening peak the water plunges back through the turbines. They use more energy than they return, so they are water batteries rather than sources — banking cheap off-peak energy, paying it out at the expensive peak, and reaching full output within minutes, which also makes them the grid's rapid-response reserve.

questions.question: Explain how a coal-fired power station generates electricity, naming each energy transformation in order from the conveyor belt to the transmission network, and account for why so little of the coal's energy becomes electricity.
questions.expected_answer: The energy changes costume four times: chemical to heat to movement to electricity. Coal arrives by conveyor, is milled finer than flour so its enormous surface area ignites instantly and burns out completely, and is blasted into a furnace running at about one thousand four hundred degrees Celsius. Kilometres of steel tubing woven into the furnace walls form the boiler, where purified water flashes into superheated steam past five hundred degrees at crushing pressure. The steam is fired at the turbine blades, spinning the shaft three thousand times a minute, and the generator on the same shaft — a massive electromagnet whirling inside copper coils — induces the current. Transformers raise the voltage to as much as four hundred kilovolts because high voltage slashes losses over long-distance cables; substations step it down near users. The exhausted steam must be condensed for another lap of the boiler — in curved cooling towers whose white plumes are water vapour, or by moving air at dry-cooled stations like Matimba and Medupi in the bone-dry Waterberg. Combustion also leaves ash and flue gases carrying carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Only about a third of the coal's chemical energy leaves as electricity because a steam cycle can only extract work from the temperature difference between its hot and cold ends: condensing the steam deliberately rejects the remaining heat to the environment, so the waste is built into the physics of the cycle, not into careless engineering.

questions.question: Evaluate whether South Africa can meet its long-term energy needs from conventional sources alone, weighing coal's advantages against its disadvantages and using Koeberg as the nuclear case study.
questions.expected_answer: Coal's advantages: reserves lasting decades give energy security; shallow seams beside the stations once made electricity among the world's cheapest, attracting smelters and heavy industry; coal delivers constant baseload; direct mining employment near ninety thousand sustains towns like Emalahleni, Middelburg and Secunda; and exports through Richards Bay earn foreign exchange. Its disadvantages: the most carbon-intensive major fuel, making South Africa the continent's heaviest emitter as carbon border taxes loom; the Highveld's ring of stations creates one of the world's most polluted airsheds, paid for in respiratory disease; wet-cooled stations evaporate scarce water while acid mine drainage bleeds from abandoned workings toward river systems like the Olifants for generations; opencast pits strip prime maize soils with rehabilitation routinely evaded; and load-shedding proved that an ageing, under-maintained fleet fails even with abundant coal, while global lenders refuse new coal finance. The nuclear case study: Koeberg's two reactors of roughly one thousand nine hundred megawatts have anchored Western Cape supply since 1984 through uranium fission — a thumbnail-sized pellet equalling about a tonne of coal — offering carbon-free operation, true baseload, tiny fuel volumes and locally mined uranium; against this stand the highest capital costs and longest build times of any generation technology, the collapse of the new-reactor plan over affordability, waste stored at Koeberg and Vaalputs that must stay isolated for millennia, and rare but catastrophic accident risk. Conclusion: conventional sources alone cannot carry the long term — coal's limits are structural and nuclear is clean but slow and expensive — so the defensible strategy is a diversified mix that includes renewables.
